questions.question: Describe the types and purposes of conservation areas in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Types: national parks (SANParks, about 19), provincial reserves (e.g. CapeNature, Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife), private and community reserves, marine protected areas, World Heritage Sites, transfrontier conservation areas (peace parks). Purposes: protect biodiversity and prevent extinction; protect ecosystem services such as water catchments; research and education; tourism jobs and income; scenery and cultural heritage (rock art); recreation. Target: 30% of land and ocean by 2030.

questions.question: Explain what a marine protected area is and how it benefits marine life and fishers.
questions.expected_answer: An area of ocean and coast where activities, especially fishing, are restricted to protect marine life and habitats; some are no-take zones, others zoned with permits. Benefits: protect breeding and nursery areas; allow overfished species to recover; spillover of adults and larvae increases catches outside; protect habitats (kelp, reefs, estuaries) and endangered species (penguins, turtles, sharks); support diving, whale watching, research. 2019: 20 new MPAs, total 41, about 5% of mainland ocean.

questions.question: Using Tsitsikamma as a case study, discuss the benefits and challenges of marine reserves.
questions.expected_answer: Established 1964 (Africa's oldest MPA), about 60 km of coast and 5 km out to sea between Plettenberg Bay and Humansdorp; now in the Garden Route National Park. Benefits: no-take zone gave more and larger reef fish (red stumpnose, roman, dageraad), nursery and spillover to nearby fisheries; tourism (Otter Trail, Storms River bridge, snorkelling) creating jobs. Challenges: local fishing communities excluded without consultation lost food and income; 2016 limited community fishing allowed, opposed by scientists - balancing conservation and community needs.
